blocks.x: Back in 1966, Gene Roddenberry's Star Trek: The Original Series birthed one of the most immensely successful and universally beloved multimedia sci-fi franchises in history. Years later, Paramount tasked him with creating a new series set in the same universe. The result of that task was Star Trek: The Next Generation, generally regarded as the best show in the whole Star Trek franchise.

It's a workplace drama in a sci-fi setting with the sort of optimistic, highly philosophical views of the future that make the Star Trek franchise so special. It's a high concept of tremendous thematic intricacy, one so layered and so timeless that The Next Generation's seven seasons and 178 episodes are still endlessly rewatchable gems today.

One of the genres that lend themselves most perfectly to a high concept that allows them to run for decades on end is the sitcom genre, which makes it unsurprising that a sci-fi sitcom as delightful as Futurama is still on the air. It's one of the most perfect sci-fi shows of the last 30 years, an animated classic that still continues to be perfectly charming all these many years later.

While many animated sitcoms end up jumping the shark in one way or another years into their runs, Futurama has managed to stay fresh, funny, and entertaining over the course of 11 seasons and 176 episodes. It's all thanks to the brilliant simplicity of its downright faultless premise, following a pizza delivery boy from 1999 who's accidentally cryogenically frozen and awakes in the year 3000.

blocks.c: Doggett (Robert Patrick), Scully (Gillian Anderson), and Skinner (Mitch Pileggi) on The X-Files.

blocks.x: The X-Files is one of the most foundational and hugely influential classics in the history of science fiction television, a procedural that's still among the most fun shows of the 1990s. The concept? An FBI agent who believes in the paranormal and a skeptical medical doctor are paired together, investigating the government's hidden vault of supernatural secrets. The result? One of the biggest cult classics in the history of television.

Indeed, The X-Files only keeps getting better and more timeless as it ages, and that's all thanks to how its high-concept premise allowed it to become one of the biggest pop-cultural phenomena of the '90s. The duality and chemistry between Mulder and Scully were the perfect anchor for that fresh idea, which is how the show was able to stay fresh for 218 episodes over the course of 11 seasons.

If there is a single show worthy of being deemed the single most influential sci-fi series in history, it's almost undoubtedly Rod Serling's The Twilight Zone, one of the most essential sci-fi shows to watch before you kick the bucket. With it, Serling completely revolutionized both sci-fi television and the anthology television format as a whole.

We're talking about five seasons and a total of 156 episodes, and though The Twilight Zone was definitely not without its share of dud episodes, many of them have gone down in history as some of the most memorable in the history of 20th-century sci-fi TV. Twilight Zone didn't invent anthology television, but it completely redefined it and crafted the undeniable blueprint for high-concept television. The medium as a whole was never the same again.

blocks.c: Catherine Tate as Donna Noble and David Tennant in 'Doctor Who.'

blocks.x: It seems that, for now, Doctor Who is going back to sleep after its 2005 and 2023 revivals (which followed the hiatus that began in 1989) ran their course. However, with it being over 60 years old, nearly 1,000 episodes long, and technically still not canceled, it's officially the longest-running science fiction show in history by a pretty decent margin.

The premise? An alien traveling through space and time with several different companions, who has the ability to regenerate into a new body after death. The very concept of regeneration only came up as a clever little trick to replace the original lead, William Hartnell, without having to cancel the series, and it's likely that the writers who came up with the idea couldn't have possibly foretold that it would allow Doctor Who to remain such a timeless, long-lasting pillar of sci-fi pop culture.

'The X-Files' (1993–2018)

The X-Files is one of the most foundational and hugely influential classics in the history of science fiction television, a procedural that's still among the most fun shows of the 1990s. The concept? An FBI agent who believes in the paranormal and a skeptical medical doctor are paired together, investigating the government's hidden vault of supernatural secrets. The result? One of the biggest cult classics in the history of television.

Indeed, The X-Files only keeps getting better and more timeless as it ages, and that's all thanks to how its high-concept premise allowed it to become one of the biggest pop-cultural phenomena of the '90s. The duality and chemistry between Mulder and Scully were the perfect anchor for that fresh idea, which is how the show was able to stay fresh for 218 episodes over the course of 11 seasons.

'The Twilight Zone' (1959–1964)

Image via CBS

If there is a single show worthy of being deemed the single most influential sci-fi series in history, it's almost undoubtedly Rod Serling's The Twilight Zone, one of the most essential sci-fi shows to watch before you kick the bucket. With it, Serling completely revolutionized both sci-fi television and the anthology television format as a whole.

We're talking about five seasons and a total of 156 episodes, and though The Twilight Zone was definitely not without its share of dud episodes, many of them have gone down in history as some of the most memorable in the history of 20th-century sci-fi TV. Twilight Zone didn't invent anthology television, but it completely redefined it and crafted the undeniable blueprint for high-concept television. The medium as a whole was never the same again.

'Doctor Who' (1963–Present)

Image via Disney+

It seems that, for now, Doctor Who is going back to sleep after its 2005 and 2023 revivals (which followed the hiatus that began in 1989) ran their course. However, with it being over 60 years old, nearly 1,000 episodes long, and technically still not canceled, it's officially the longest-running science fiction show in history by a pretty decent margin.

The premise? An alien traveling through space and time with several different companions, who has the ability to regenerate into a new body after death. The very concept of regeneration only came up as a clever little trick to replace the original lead, William Hartnell, without having to cancel the series, and it's likely that the writers who came up with the idea couldn't have possibly foretold that it would allow Doctor Who to remain such a timeless, long-lasting pillar of sci-fi pop culture.
